newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Ample liquidity seen keeping Seoul stocks buoyant.
newsitem.headline: Ample liquidity seen keeping Seoul stocks buoyant.

text.p: South Korean stocks are seen climbing in the near future because of high liquidity in the aftermath of the Hanbo Steel Co debt crisis, brokers said on Wednesday.
But they said sentiment could sour again unless supported by economic fundamentals.

After initially contracting on news that Hanbo Steel had defaulted on loan payments after piling up more than five trillion won ($5.8 billion) of debt, brokers said the market was riding high on the government's release of trillions of won into the money market to prevent similar corporate failures.
They said investors were now paying little attention to the Hanbo scandal, which is seen to have become more a political issue than a business one.
"Ample money supply has been the main impetus pushing the stock market higher and will continue to be so for the time being," said Chang Keun-ho, a broker at Daishin Securities.
Brokers said a dearth of upcoming new issues would also boost the market.

More than six trillion won ($6.9 billion) was pumped into the money market to prevent the Hanbo crisis from causing a chain reaction of corporate failures and to meet rising money demand before the Lunar New Year holidays on February 7-9.
"About 200 billion won from the money supply has already flowed into the stock market and another 300 billion will come in by the end of the month," said Choo Hee-yup of Dongwon Securities.
Brokers said the composite stock index has gained about five percent since January 24 when Hanbo Steel Co, flagship of the Hanbo Group, defaulted on its loan obligations.
On Wednesday, the Seoul stock market composite index ended at a provisional 712.50 points, down 0.93 of a point.

State prosecutors have arrested top government officials, including a close associate of President Kim Young-sam, on charges of taking kickbacks from Hanbo in return for pressuring banks into giving loans to its steel unit. On Wednesday, Home Affairs Minister Kim Woo-suk resigned after being questioned in connection with the loans.
"If the Bank of Korea does not tighten money supply, the index could test 750-770 this month," Choo said.
Brokers said the central bank showed no signs that it planned to absorb liquidity in circulation when it injected another 1.26 trillion won on Tuesday through repurchase agreements.
Yields for benchmark three-year corporate bonds dropped to 11.95 percent on Wednesday from 12.05/10 percent last week.
Customer deposits with securities houses rose to three trillion won from about 2.88 trillion won late in January.
"It is not too optimistic to expect a rally in financial and construction shares, which have so far been ignored in recent rises," said Kim Heung-shik of Hyundai Securities.
But brokers said such rallies, underpinned largely by high liquidity, would be short-lived unless economic fundamentals improved.
"The central bank will have to hit the brakes on money supply sometime soon to curb inflationary pressure," said a Daewoo Securities broker. "Then bubbles will begin bursting."
Brokers said the ballooning trade deficit could pose an obstacle as exports were unlikely to recover soon.
South Korea posted the largest-ever monthly deficit of $3.48 billion in January, compared with a shortfall of $2.13 billion a year earlier.
